steps.user_message: I'm preparing my 2024 taxes and could use your help. Situation: married filing jointly, Phoenix AZ. W-2 from Acme Corp: $82,350. Side income: $14,600 from data analysis (3 clients). Interest $2,340 (Chase savings), dividends $440 (Robinhood). Home office: 110 sq ft, rent $1,820/month, apartment 780 sq ft. Deductions: student loan interest $4,250 (Sallie Mae, 2017–2020); charity $2,000 to Local United Way have the receipt; unreimbursed expenses $950. Can you help me figure out deductions, standard vs itemized, and home office treatment—and which forms to use?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — this is enough to give a clear plan and a good estimate. I’ll (1) explain how each item is reported, (2) show how to treat the home office and the two deduction methods, (3) compare itemizing vs. taking the standard deduction, (4) list the federal (and a note about Arizona) forms you’ll need, and (5) give next steps and questions if you want a tighter estimate.

Summary of your situation (what you gave)
- Filing status: Married filing jointly (Phoenix, AZ)  
- W-2 wages (Acme): $82,350  
- Self-employment (data analysis, 3 clients): $14,600 gross  
- Interest (Chase savings): $2,340  
- Dividends (Robinhood): $440  
- Home: apartment 780 sq ft; dedicated home office 110 sq ft; rent $1,820/mo → $21,840/yr  
- Student loan interest paid: $4,250 (Sallie Mae) — you should have Form 1098-E for 2024 interest actually paid  
- Charitable cash donations: $2,000 (you have receipts)  
- “Unreimbursed expenses” $950 — need to know whether these are business expenses for your side gig or unreimbursed employee expenses from Acme

1) How each item is reported (federal)
- W-2 wages: reported on Form 1040 (W-2 attached).  
- Self-employment income: report gross and expenses on Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business). Net profit from Schedule C flows to Form 1040 (Schedule 1).  
- Self-employment tax: pay Social Security/Medicare on net SE earnings — calculate on Schedule SE. SE tax is approximately 15.3% of ~92.35% of net earnings; half of that SE tax is an above-the-line deduction (reported on Schedule 1).  
- Interest & dividends: report on Form 1040. Because your total interest + ordinary dividends = $2,780 (> $1,500), you must also file Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends).  
- Student loan interest: reported as an adjustment to income (Schedule 1) up to $2,500 maximum; it phases out at higher MAGI (see note below). Even though you paid $4,250, the deductible amount is capped. You need Form 1098‑E from Sallie Mae showing interest paid in the tax year.  
- Charitable donations: deductible on Schedule A if you itemize. Cash donations generally are fully deductible (subject to AGI limits), but only if you itemize.  
- Unreimbursed employee expenses: NOT deductible for most employees (suspended under TCJA through 2025). If the $950 are business expenses for your self-employed data work, they belong on Schedule C and reduce your self-employment income. Please confirm which they are.  
- Home office: reported on Schedule C as a business expense if the space is used exclusively and regularly for your self-employment. See next section for methods.

2) Home office — two methods and recommendation for your numbers
You qualify for a home office deduction for the side gig if the 110 sq ft area is used regularly and exclusively for the business (and is your principal place of business).

Two ways to compute:
- Simplified method: $5 per square foot, up to 300 sq ft → 110 sq ft × $5 = $550. Easy, no allocation of utilities or rent needed.  
- Regular (actual) method: allocate a percentage of actual home expenses to the business. Your business percentage = 110 / 780 = 14.10%. Applying that to rent: $21,840 × 14.10% ≈ $3,078 (you can also allocate a portion of utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., if you have them).  

Which to use here: based on rent alone, the actual method yields ~ $3,078 vs. $550 simplified. Actual method is larger for your facts. That home office deduction is deducted on Schedule C (reduces your net business profit). Note: the home office deduction cannot create a business loss that is disallowed because of passive rules — in self-employment situations you can generally use it to reduce net SE income, but if it puts the business into a loss, different rules/limits can apply.

3) Quick estimated computation (one assumption set)
Assume the $950 are business expenses (if they are employee unreimbursed expenses, ignore them for Schedule C). Using the actual home office allocation:

- Gross self-employment income: 14,600  
- Home office (actual, rent share): ≈ 3,078  
- Other business expenses: 950  
- Net Schedule C profit ≈ 14,600 − 3,078 − 950 = 10,572

Self-employment tax (approx):
- Net earnings subject to SE tax = 10,572 × 0.9235 ≈ 9,765  
- SE tax ≈ 9,765 × 0.153 ≈ $1,493  
- Deduction (half SE tax) ≈ $746 (above-the-line)

Adjustments to income:
- Student loan interest deduction — up to $2,500 (assuming your MAGI is below the phaseout range; see note)  
- Half SE tax ≈ $746

Total income before adjustments = W-2 82,350 + net business 10,572 + interest 2,340 + dividends 440 = ≈ $95,702  
Less above-the-line adjustments ≈ 2,500 + 746 = $3,246 → Estimated AGI ≈ $92,456

Itemized vs standard:
- Your itemized deductible items that you listed: charitable donations $2,000 + possibly state income tax paid (unknown from W-2 box 17). Unreimbursed employee expenses are not deductible. That gives you about $2,000 in itemized deductions (plus any state tax you actually paid — check W-2 Box 17 and any 1099s or estimated state tax payments). The standard deduction for married filing jointly is significantly higher than $2,000, so you will almost certainly take the standard deduction. (If you have substantial state tax withholdings, mortgage interest, or more charitable gifts, re-check).

Note on QBI (Qualified Business Income) deduction:
- With your income level, you’re likely below the income thresholds where complex limits apply, so you should be eligible for the 20% QBI deduction on qualified business income from the Schedule C. Roughly 20% × net business income (after the half-SE-tax adjustment rules) could be available — in the rough example above that’s on the order of $2,100–$2,200. The QBI deduction is reported via Form 8995 (or 8995-A if complex) and then on Form 1040 as a deduction.

4) Forms you will need (federal)
- Form 1040 — main return.  
- Schedule 1 (Additional Income and Adjustments) — to report business income adjustments (in some years Schedule 1 is used; the important point is student loan interest and half SE tax are adjustments to income).  
- Schedule C — report your side income and business expenses (including the home office deduction).  
- Schedule SE — calculate self-employment tax.  
- Schedule B — required because your combined interest + ordinary dividends exceed $1,500.  
- Form 8995 (or 8995-A) — to calculate the QBI (20%) deduction, if you claim it.  
- Schedule A — only if you itemize (seems unlikely with $2,000 charity only).  
- Arizona state return — Arizona Form 140 (or the correct current AZ individual return form for the tax year). State filing will take your federal AGI as a starting point; include any Arizona-specific credits or adjustments. Check for state withholding on W-2 (Box 17) or AZ estimated payments.

5) Other practical notes and records to gather
- 1099-INT from Chase for interest, 1099-DIV from Robinhood for dividends. (If you received any 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC from clients, gather those.)  
- 1098-E from Sallie Mae showing interest paid in 2024 (that determines the actual amount eligible for the student loan interest deduction). If the 1098-E shows less than $2,500, your deductible amount cannot exceed that.  
- W-2 from Acme (check state tax withheld box).  
- Receipts for the $2,000 charitable contributions.  
- Documentation that the 110 sq ft space is used exclusively and regularly for business (photos, floor plan, dates used) in case of IRS questions. Also any utility/renter’s insurance bills if you use the actual method beyond rent.  
- If the $950 are business expenses (software, subscriptions, supplies, travel related to the side gig), list/collect receipts and classify them for Schedule C.

6) Items needing clarification from you (so I can give a tighter, line-by-line tax estimate)
- Are the $950 “unreimbursed expenses” employee expenses (from your W-2 job) or business expenses for your side gig? (If employee — not deductible; if business — they go on Schedule C.)  
- Did you have any Arizona state tax withheld (W-2 box 17) or pay any AZ estimated tax?  
- Do you have 1099s from clients, or did they not issue 1099s?  
- Do you want me to run estimated federal tax owed (income tax + self-employment tax) using the numbers above and an assumed standard deduction? If so, I’ll compute an approximate federal tax liability.

7) Next steps / recommended actions
- Gather the small set of forms listed above (W-2, 1099-INT, 1099-DIV, 1098-E, any 1099-NEC).  
- Confirm whether $950 is business-related.  
- Decide to claim the home office actual method (bigger deduction given your rent) — collect rent and utility statements; if you prefer simplicity, you can use simplified $550 instead. I can compute the exact tax difference both ways.  
- If you want an estimate of total federal tax owed (and Arizona), tell me whether to treat the $950 as business expenses and whether you want me to use the actual home office number (~$3,078) or the simplified method.

If you want, I’ll:
- Run the tighter numbers and estimate your federal tax (income tax + self-employment tax + how much you might owe/receive) once you confirm the $950 classification and whether you want actual or simplified home office.
